expectations.text: The reply opens with a clear recommendation the council can act on, without labelling or attacking the alderman.
expectations.evidence: "My advice: don't buy this system as specified, and don't promise go-live in six months. Instead, offer the alderman a six-month plan that measurably improves enforcement, with a decision point at the end." Respectful: "The council has a real point: fraud erodes support for the safety net"; it also suggests a private conversation and offers a ready-to-use line.

expectations.text: The reply names the precedent and what went wrong: the Dutch childcare benefits scandal or similar risk-scoring cases, with bias, presumed guilt and no meaningful human or legal check.
expectations.evidence: Rotterdam: "Its own documents showed the model was only 50% better than random selection. The city paused it in 2021 over bias it couldn't remove." Amsterdam: "The bias had come back in a new direction, and the model flagged more people than caseworkers without finding the right cases any better." SyRI: "struck down... as insufficiently transparent and verifiable"; "the childcare benefits scandal showed where risk profiling ends." Bias and the failed legal check are explicit. The childcare case itself is thin, but the Rotterdam/Amsterdam detail covers the mechanism. Verified against Lighthouse Reports and MIT Technology Review.

expectations.text: The reply questions the "90% accurate" claim: with a low share of real fraud, most people flagged may have done nothing wrong; it asks for false-positive rates and bias tests across groups and proxies such as nationality, age or postcode.
expectations.evidence: "a model that flags nobody is 95% accurate. A 90%-accurate model that sends the top 10% to investigators flags 100 of every 1,000 recipients. Only 25 of those 100 are real cases; the other 75 committed no fraud" (checks: TP 25, FP 75, FN 25, TN 875 → 90%). Asks for "the hit rate within the top 10%, the error rates by group (nationality, gender, age, single parents), and whether it was measured on your data"; proxies via "DUO's simple rules (distance to parents, type of education) still discriminated indirectly".

expectations.text: The reply flags the legal floor for counsel: the GDPR (legal basis, purpose limitation for debt-counselling data, a data protection impact assessment, automated decisions) and the AI Act's high-risk rules for public benefits, with their timing.
expectations.evidence: "The AI Act's ban on social scoring has applied since February 2025" with the Commission's welfare-fraud example (verified via the FPF summary); "very likely high-risk, because it concerns public benefits. The high-risk obligations, including a fundamental rights impact assessment, apply from 2 December 2027"; "The GDPR adds a DPIA and purpose limitation on the debt-counselling data, and after the CJEU's SCHUFA ruling a score that largely decides who is investigated may count as an automated decision"; "First you need a legal basis"; "get a written view from your FG and legal team before anything is procured."

expectations.text: The reply offers alternatives that address causes, such as simpler rules, help with applications or better data quality, noting that many errors are mistakes rather than fraud.
expectations.evidence: "Investigate a random sample... deliberate fraud, honest mistakes with complex rules, or the municipality's own errors"; "fix what causes errors. Simplify reporting changes in income or household. Contact people as soon as an Inlichtingenbureau signal arrives instead of reclaiming months later. Use plain-language letters. Fewer errors mean fewer investigations."

expectations.text: The reply sets safeguards for anything that goes ahead: a human decides, people are told and can object, an independent audit, publication in the algorithm register, and criteria for stopping.
expectations.evidence: Has: "An investigator always decides, and no payment is ever stopped on a score alone"; "registered in the Algoritmeregister"; "Fix the stop criteria before it starts, add an independent audit and involve the cliëntenraad." Missing: any safeguard that affected residents are told they were selected and can object or appeal. "Selection you can explain" and "published rules" give policy-level transparency, not individual notice and an objection route. One of the five required elements is absent.

overall_quality.evidence: Tight, accurate and well-sourced. The Rotterdam and Amsterdam specifics, cause-fixing alternatives, the Participatiewet in balans hook and a ready private line to the alderman make it very usable. It only lacks resident notice/objection and a fuller vendor-question list.

factual_errors.evidence: Verified: Rotterdam 2017–2021, ~30,000, top 10%, 'only 50 percent more accurate' than random, pulled in 2021 over bias it couldn't remove; Amsterdam stopped Nov 2023, ~€535,000 (€500k + €35k), flagged more without better hits; Participatieraad objected in March 2022; social-scoring ban Feb 2025 with the welfare example; high-risk from 2 Dec 2027; Participatiewet in balans partly in force 1 Jan 2026 with 'vertrouwen en de menselijke maat' central; DUO indirect discrimination and random checks since June 2023. Minor: 'about seven months after the planned go-live' is nearer six (late May to 2 Dec 2027).

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: Prospective decision; no bad outcome in the prompt.

best_insight.value: The random sample is 'your only unbiased test data'. It also ties the advice to the Participatiewet in balans (trust and the human dimension), which gives the CIO a policy argument the council already signed up to.
best_insight.evidence: 'Months 1–3: measure' and the 'It hurts the people you serve' bullet

suggestions.assertion: The reply names the precedent and what went wrong: the Dutch childcare benefits scandal or similar risk-scoring cases, with bias, presumed guilt and no meaningful human or legal check.
suggestions.reason: Bundles three failure mechanisms (bias, presumed guilt, no human/legal check) without saying how many are needed; samples covered different subsets. Name the minimum, or split it. It also doesn't check that the precedent is described accurately: one sample gave a wrong year for Amsterdam's Smart Check and would still pass.

suggestions.assertion: The reply flags the legal floor for counsel: the GDPR (legal basis, purpose limitation for debt-counselling data, a data protection impact assessment, automated decisions) and the AI Act's high-risk rules for public benefits, with their timing.
suggestions.reason: A long conjunctive list (legal basis, purpose limitation, DPIA, automated decisions, AI Act high-risk, timing). It discriminates well, but it leaves out the AI Act Art. 5(1)(c) social-scoring ban, which is the strongest legal point for scoring on debt-counselling data. The Commission's guidelines list welfare fraud scoring on unrelated-context data as an example. Consider adding it.

No assertion covers the chilling effect on residents seeking debt help, or the label/feedback-loop problem (a model trained on past investigations learns where investigators looked). These were the most decision-relevant insights in the strongest samples.

No assertion checks for the closest municipal precedents (Rotterdam's identical score-everyone/top-10% design; Amsterdam's 'by the book' Smart Check that still failed). It also doesn't check for involving the cliëntenraad, works council and investigators before choosing the tool.

eval_feedback.overall: Strong, compact and accurate; it misses only the resident notice-and-objection safeguard.
